title: Decision: ship pkix-ct-google (reversed an earlier wont-do)
description: Records why a per-program CT anchor crate for Google was considered, started, and abandoned. See notes for the full reasoning and the verbatim policy text.
notes:
REVERSED 2026-11-24, same day. The crate was built. This record is kept rather than deleted because the reasoning that led to abandoning it was wrong in an instructive way.

## What this bead originally concluded

That pkix-ct-google should not exist, on the strength of Google's acceptable-use policy:

  "Chrome's CT log lists may not be used to facilitate CT enforcement in TLS
   clients other than Chrome without explicit written permission from Chrome's
   CT team."

The argument was that a crate making the list turnkey points at the prohibited use, and would make the prohibited configuration the frictionless default.

## Why that was wrong

Two errors, one structural and one about what the crate actually does.

1. AN AUP IS NOT A LICENCE ON A PUBLISHED FACT. An acceptable-use policy takes its force from a service agreement -- something accepted as a condition of access to a service. Retrieving an unauthenticated public URL accepts nothing and forms no such agreement. And where a rightsholder has copyright or trademark to assert, they assert it; a policy statement doing that work instead tends to indicate neither reaches the artifact. A public key is a number.

   Treating the AUP as decisive gave a vendor's published wish the force of law, and then declined to build something useful on that basis. That is the error worth remembering: deferring to the authority-shape of an instrument rather than asking what it actually binds.

2. THE CRATE SHIPS THE KEY, NOT THE LIST. This matters more than the first point and was simply missed. The LIST is policy -- it encodes which logs Google's program trusts, and it churns weekly. The KEY says only who signed. Shipping it commits a consumer to nothing about Google's inclusion criteria, only to being able to tell whether a list they fetched is the one Google published.

   So the "corporate super anchor" framing did not apply in the first place. And on Google's own terms the crate serves the audience the AUP expressly permits: monitors, auditors and certificate submitters all need exactly this key, because verifying the list signature is how they know they have the real list.

## What survived

The warning inside the policy, which is real and holds whoever has permission: a client pinning Chrome's log LIST inherits Chrome's inclusion and retirement decisions on Chrome's schedule, with no notice. A stale copy means either rejecting good certificates whose log is newer than the list, or believing CT is enforced while checking against a set that no longer describes the ecosystem. Neither announces itself.

That argues for refreshing the list -- which is precisely what being able to verify a signature makes safe -- and not against being able to check one.

Both the policy and this warning are now documented in pkix-ct-google and in pkix-ct's module docs, as facts a consumer should know, with the judgement left to the operator.

## The general principle, restated

Unchanged and still useful:

  Where there is no choice, shipping an anchor is shipping a fact.
  Where there is a choice, shipping one is taking sides.

What the reversal adds is a prior question: ask whether the artifact is the policy or merely the thing that authenticates it. IANA's root KSK and Google's log-list signing key are both of the second kind. Google's log LIST is of the first, and is still not shipped -- not on anyone's permission, but because a weekly-churning policy document does not belong pinned in a crate.
close_reason: Decision recorded, not built. Google's acceptable-use policy prohibits using its CT log lists to facilitate CT enforcement in non-Chrome TLS clients without written permission from Chrome's CT team, which is the primary use a pkix-ct-google crate would have made frictionless. Documented in pkix-ct instead; 'the caller supplies the key' stands as the permanent answer for vendor anchors. See notes.
